meta.description: Not Einstein. The joke is French and predates him — credited to Alexandre Dumas fils in an 1865 dictionary, which we read in the scan.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Difference Between Stupidity and Genius Is That Genius Has Its Limits'?
meta.ogDescription: A French epigram credited to Alexandre Dumas fils in 1865, well before Einstein was born. He was attached to it by 1994.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — adapted from Alexandre Dumas fils
answer.sourceLine: The joke is French and older than Einstein. Larousse’s Grand dictionnaire universel du XIXe siècle, in its entry for bêtise (stupidity), prints: “Une chose qui m’humilie profondément est de voir que le génie humain a des limites, quand la bêtise humaine n’en a pas”, credited to “Alex. Dum.” Quote Investigator ↗ credits Alexandre Dumas fils and finds no substantive evidence for Einstein, whose name is attached only by 1994.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Grand dictionnaire universel du XIX<sup>e</sup> siècle, volume 2, entry “Bêtise”
Pierre Larousse, Paris. Quote Investigator dates the volume circa 1865; the Bibliothèque nationale de France scan at the Internet Archive is catalogued 1866.
“Alex. Dum.” — probably Alexandre Dumas fils, the dramatist of La Dame aux Camélias, rather than his father the novelist
“Some of Dumas’s Maxims”, in The Travelers’ Record, 1890, crediting a French newspaper: “What distresses me is to see that human genius has limits and human stupidity none.”
1994 — the earliest Einstein instance Quote Investigator locates, in a Cedar Rapids, Iowa newspaper

source.excerpt: Une chose qui m'humilie profondément est de voir que le génie humain a des limites, quand la bêtise humaine n'en a pas. (Alex. Dum.)
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “Alexandre Dumas, fils, can be credited with the expression given in the 1865 citation”, that Elbert Hubbard popularised a 1906 variant, and that “there is no substantive evidence that Albert Einstein said or wrote any instances of the expression”. It also notes the saying is listed under “Probably Not By Einstein” in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

We verified the dictionary entry rather than relying on the citation. We downloaded the full scanned text of volume 2 of the Grand dictionnaire universel ↗ from the Internet Archive, found the Bêtise entry, and read the sentence there in place, with its “(Alex. Dum.)” credit intact — exactly as Quote Investigator reports it.

The English side is well attested and old. Quote Investigator’s earliest English instance is an 1890 list headed “Some of Dumas’s Maxims” in The Travelers’ Record, and an 1891 Phrenological Journal printing names “A. Dumas, fils” explicitly — which is what settles which Dumas is meant.

The modern shape came later. The publisher Elbert Hubbard ↗ printed “Genius may have its limitations, but stupidity is not thus handicapped” in 1906, and the wording closest to today’s — “The difference between genius and stupidity is that genius has limitations” — appears unattributed in an Indiana newspaper in 1961, more than thirty years before anyone thought of Einstein.
source.excerptNote: One possible English rendering: “One thing that humbles me deeply is to see that human genius has its limits while human stupidity does not.” The entry is a list of epigrams on stupidity; this one sits between a Beauchêne and a Madame de Girardin.

author.name: Alexandre Dumas fils
author.heading: About Alexandre Dumas fils
author.bio: Alexandre Dumas fils was the son of the novelist Alexandre Dumas père, author of The Count of Monte Cristo and The Three Musketeers — a shared name that has caused two centuries of confusion. The son’s own reputation rests on La Dame aux Camélias (1848), the novel he adapted for the stage and which Verdi turned into La traviata. He wrote drama of social argument, and epigrams sharp enough that French dictionaries quoted him as an authority on the language while he was still alive.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A nineteenth-century French epigram that acquired a twentieth-century physicist.

items.why: The saying was in print in French more than a decade before Einstein was born and circulating in English from 1890. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive evidence he said it, and its earliest Einstein instance is from 1994.
Credited “Alex. Dum.” in the bêtise entry of Larousse’s Grand dictionnaire universel, and named as “A. Dumas, fils” in an 1891 English printing. We read the dictionary entry in the scan ↗.
Hubbard printed the “handicapped” version in his magazine The Philistine in 1906, and it was reprinted as his epigram the following year. He sharpened the joke; he did not invent it.

Quote Investigator notes a 1963 item that used Einstein as an example of genius alongside the saying without attributing it to him — the kind of adjacency that inattentive readers convert into authorship.

misattribution.truthLine: The epigram belongs to Alexandre Dumas fils, by way of an 1860s French dictionary — as Quote Investigator establishes ↗ and as the scanned volume confirms.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line has been funny in three languages and at least five wordings for over 150 years, which is the real reason it keeps finding new authors. A joke that survives translation is a joke nobody needs a source for — and that is exactly the condition under which a famous name gets attached.

Einstein is the natural magnet because the epigram is about genius. Attaching it to the century’s emblem of genius makes it self-referential and a little humble, which is a better story than “a French dramatist said something clever in the 1860s”. The better story is not the true one.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology shows an unusually clear case of an aphorism evolving in public: an 1886 French journal printing it in quotation marks with no attribution because the joke was already common; an 1899 Indiana paper reprinting it as something it had run years earlier; a 1907 anonymous newspaper list of “differences”; a 1909 doctor using it in a medical journal; a Jamaican paper in 1939 aiming it at nine legislators.

By 1961 an Indiana filler item had it in essentially the modern form and still with no author. Einstein does not appear until 1994 — which is the point: the sentence had done a century of work anonymously before it needed a genius to sign it.
context.pull: In print in French more than a decade before Einstein was born.

sourcesVerified.claim: Alexandre Dumas fils can be credited with the expression given in the 1865 citation; Elbert Hubbard popularised the 1906 version; there is no substantive evidence Einstein said or wrote it, and the earliest Einstein instance is from 1994.

The entry "Betise" in volume 2 of the Grand dictionnaire universel du XIXe siecle contains "Une chose qui m'humilie profondement est de voir que le genie humain a des limites, quand la betise humaine n'en a pas. (Alex. Dum.)"
Alexandre Dumas fils lived 27 July 1824 to 27 November 1895 and was a French author and playwright best known for La Dame aux Camelias.
